Prices fell, so you stocked up? Here's how that deal can quietly hurt you.
Ronnie runs a keeraana store. His wholesaler says, oil and daal are ten percent cheaper today.
So Ronnie puts all his cash, and an overdraft, into stock. Fifteen laakh rupees.
Normally, his shop runs like a wheel. Cash, stock, sales, and cash again. Every fifteen days.
Now the wheel jams. That extra stock takes four months to sell.
And the overdraft charges nine thousand rupees, every month.
His one laakh saving? Interest ate thirty six thousand. Expired stock, forty thousand more.
And with no cash left, he couldn't restock his fast sellers. Customers went next door.
This is exactly what financial ratios catch, early.
Quick ratio. Cash you can use, against bills you owe. Around one is healthy. Ronnie's fell to point one.
Inventory days. How long stock sits on the shelf. His jumped from fifteen to fifty.
Too low, and you can't pay bills. Too high, and money sits idle. Both mean trouble.
